tldr: We present Alloy, an open-source physics engine for robot learning that unifies rigid robots, cloth, cables, liquids, granular materials, and soft bodies in a single scene with fast GPU parallelization. It also provides detailed diagnostics and Model Context Protocol (MCP) support so that AI coding agents can run learning tasks autonomously.
hero_caption: Diverse scenes simulated in Alloy: (a) pouring water with a robot arm, (b) routing a cable through clips, (c) inserting a battery into a spring-loaded holder, and (d) 1,024 parallel worlds running on a single GPU. Tasks involving cloth and fluids, alongside rigid bodies, can run in parallel at scale.
overview:
Robots in homes and factories face countless tasks with non-rigid materials, such as pouring water, folding towels, or routing cables. Training policies for these via reinforcement learning requires millions of trials, but current simulators for robot learning are mostly specialized for parallel rigid-body computation. Handling fluids or cloth usually meant bringing in a second solver, handwriting bridge code to glue them together, and struggling to detect simulation failures.

To solve this, the authors developed Alloy, a physics engine that handles rigid robots, cloth, cables, liquids, granular materials, and soft bodies through a single Python interface. Users simply specify physical properties using a material card. Inside Alloy, a router automatically assigns objects to suitable solvers—such as MuJoCo Warp, Newton's VBD or MPM, or Alloy's own SPH fluid solver. The solvers couple within each control step via proxy bodies, and Alloy automatically selects the right sub-stepping time intervals based on stiffness.

Alloy is also designed from the ground up to be driven by coding agents. Documentation is bundled inside the package, every error message suggests a specific fix, and the engine is exposed as tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

In experiments, a coding agent (Claude Opus 5.5) with no prior knowledge of Alloy set up environments from scratch on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU. It successfully trained policies for quadruped walking, cable lifting, and water pouring. The engine also demonstrated high throughput across 1,024 parallel worlds, close agreement with analytical solutions, and rock-solid reliability with zero block tower collapses.
contributions: Built a unified architecture that handles rigid robots, cloth, cables, fluids, granular materials, and soft bodies with a single scene description and Python interface.
Achieved stable two-way coupling between different solvers inside every control step using proxy bodies and automatic sub-step selection.
Introduced real-time world health grades (OK, DEGRADED, INVALID) across parallel simulations, helping distinguish a failure of the physics from a failure of the policy.
Provided agent-ready interfaces—including in-package documentation, fix-suggesting error messages, a JSON CLI, and an MCP server—allowing AI coding agents to operate self-sufficiently.

sections.heading: Why does robot learning need a new multi-material physics engine?
sections.summary: Real-world robotic tasks are full of non-rigid materials, but existing large-scale simulators specialize in rigid bodies, requiring manual glue code to bring in other materials. Alloy solves this and gives AI coding agents an environment they can drive autonomously.
sections.details:
Pouring water, wiping kitchen counters, routing cables in factories, folding laundry—practical robot applications are filled with deformable items and fluids. Learning these skills with simulation-based reinforcement learning requires both high-fidelity physics tailored to each material (like cloth drape or fluid flow) and massive GPU parallelism to run thousands of environments at once.

Existing tools, however, split these two needs. Scaled training engines excel at rigid bodies, while cloth and fluid solvers lived in separate programs. Researchers had to write their own bridge code, manually tune time steps, and constantly watch for exploding simulations.

At the same time, coding agents (LLMs) are increasingly writing simulation code instead of humans. To work effectively, agents need concise documentation packaged right with the code, error messages that explain how to fix the problem rather than just stating it, and a way to tell whether a poor run is due to a bad policy or broken physics.

Alloy was built to tackle all of these challenges. It lets users define multiple materials in a single scene, handles automatic solver routing and coupling, evaluates world-by-world health grades, and exposes agent-ready tooling. Released under the Apache-2.0 open-source license, it can be installed easily via `pip install alloy-engine`.

sections.heading: Unifying existing solvers under one roof without reinventing the wheel
sections.summary: Rather than building every solver from scratch, Alloy builds on top of proven solvers like MuJoCo Warp and Newton. It adds an outer integration layer for automatic routing, coupling, and agent tooling.
sections.details:
To place this work in context, let us review existing simulation technologies.

### Rigid-body engines and learning environments
MuJoCo is the industry standard for simulating articulated robots with contact. GPU-accelerated versions like MuJoCo Warp, along with frameworks like MuJoCo Playground, Orbit (now Isaac Lab), and ManiSkill3, have made it possible to train legged locomotion in minutes via GPU parallelism.

### Deformable and fluid solvers
For cloth and soft bodies, Vertex Block Descent (VBD) solves per-vertex problems, remaining stable even at large time steps. Liquids are commonly modeled with SPH (a particle method) to conserve volume, while sand and pastes use MPM (Material Point Method). Newton packages these solvers on top of Warp, and Genesis also aims to unify multiple materials.

### Where Alloy stands
Alloy does not reinvent these solvers; it builds on them. Rigid robots run on MuJoCo Warp (or MuJoCo on CPU), cloth, soft bodies, and elastic rods run on Newton's VBD, sand and paste run on Newton's MPM, and liquids run on Alloy's custom SPH solver. Alloy's true contribution is the layer wrapping them together. It provides a single scene description, automatic routing, coupled steps with dynamic time-stepping, per-world health checks, cameras across all worlds, and agent tooling—sparing researchers from handwriting glue code. MuJoCo model files (MJCF) are also supported natively.

sections.heading: How Alloy works: from material cards to automatic coupling and health diagnostics
sections.summary: Objects in a scene are registered alongside physical material cards, and a router automatically assigns them to the best solver. Different solvers couple bidirectionally every step via proxy bodies, and broken worlds are automatically detected and frozen.
sections.details:
Alloy's architecture (as of version 0.1.2) is built for ease of use and robustness.

### 3.1 Scenes and material cards
Users add objects by providing their geometry and a material card—a small file specifying measured physical properties like density, stiffness, and friction. Users do not need to choose a solver. Simply placing a robot arm and a water container into the same scene is enough.

### 3.2 Routing
During scene setup, the router follows a fixed sequence of physical tests to assign each object to a solver route. It first checks for static objects, then determines the phase (gas, liquid, or granular), classifies the geometry (rod, sheet, or volume), and evaluates compliance. It checks whether the body deforms or bends past a threshold under expected grip forces. If it passes, it is treated as rigid; if it flexes, it routes to a deformable solver. Numerical margins and thresholds explaining the decision are recorded and inspectable via the API.

### 3.3 Solver coupling
When different solvers coexist, they couple through proxy bodies. The geometry and velocity of a rigid body appear as a proxy in the deformable solver. When the deformable solver calculates contact forces, the opposing force feeds back to the rigid body. For lightweight liquids with negligible back-reaction, one-way coupling without force feedback is supported. When strong coupling occurs with heavier counterparts, iterations run with Aitken acceleration to adapt the relaxation factor. Worlds freeze as they converge, ensuring determinism independent of other worlds in the batch.

### 3.4 Automatic time-stepping
The control period (e.g., 10 ms) is divided into sub-step intervals $h = 2^{-j}$, determined dynamically from interface effective mass $m_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and contact stiffness $k_c$. Stiff, light contacts exchange data frequently, while soft, heavy contacts take larger steps. If watchdogs monitoring energy conservation or interface drift catch an anomaly, that specific world rolls back to its previous step and recalculates with a finer time step (escalation).

### 3.5 Per-world health grading
Across thousands of parallel worlds, simulation instabilities can occasionally arise. Alloy tracks non-finite values (like NaNs), interpenetrations, excessive velocities, and abrupt energy jumps at every step. It grades each world as OK, DEGRADED, or INVALID. Invalid worlds are rolled back to their last healthy state and frozen, preventing reinforcement learning from exploiting simulation glitches (reward hacking).

### 3.6 Parallel execution, cameras, and robot assets
By capturing and replaying CUDA graphs, Alloy minimizes GPU-host communication overhead for ultra-fast parallel runs. Each world supports cameras providing depth and segmentation, following the Gymnasium vector environment standard. It ships out of the box with nine robots—including Franka, UR10e, Unitree G1/H1-2/Go2, and the LEAP hand—along with pre-configured environments and material cards.

### 3.7 AI coding agent interface
Documentation is bundled directly inside the package, ensuring agents read instructions matching the exact version running. Every error message comes with an actionable suggestion detailing which field to fix and how. Agents can also operate the simulator directly through JSON-based CLI tools and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server.

sections.heading: From zero-shot AI agent training to reliability testing
sections.summary: AI agents with no prior knowledge of Alloy trained walking and pouring policies on a single GPU. Alloy also demonstrated strong scaling across parallel worlds, high depth-camera throughput, theoretical accuracy, and stable block tower tests.
sections.details:
Several experiments evaluated Alloy's practical performance and accuracy.

### 4.1 Cold tests with AI coding agents
Coding agents (Claude Opus 5.5) with no prior knowledge of Alloy were placed in fresh virtual machines with a single NVIDIA L4 GPU to see if they could write code and train policies autonomously.
- **Walking**: Trained Unitree Go2 for velocity tracking using PPO. After 400 iterations, the policy withstood a 150 N push disturbance for 0.1 s—higher than the maximum 113 N seen during training—staying upright in roughly 250 out of 256 episodes.
- **Cable lift**: The agent designed and implemented the task itself, achieving a 95.7% success rate (lifting the entire cable centerline by at least 3 cm) in about 30 minutes of training.
- **Pouring**: Pouring water from a bottle into a bowl (with at least 75% entering) succeeded in 118 out of 128 episodes after ~38.5 minutes of training. In an independently crafted cup-pouring task by another agent, the success rate reached 256 out of 256 after ~70 minutes.
- **Imitation**: Collecting demonstrations and running behavioral cloning (BC) achieved 256 out of 256 successes on a pick-and-place task after just 66 seconds of training.

### 4.2 Throughput across worlds
Scaling world counts on a single L4 GPU demonstrated clear parallel efficiency. From 1 to 64 worlds, throughput grew roughly 39x for a Franka arm scene, ~20x for cotton cloth on a table, and ~13x for pouring 200 ml of liquid. For dropping rigid bodies into a bin, throughput scaled ~377x from 1 to 512 worlds.

### 4.3 Depth camera throughput
For vision-based learning, rendering depth images across 1,024 parallel worlds in the Franka scene sustained throughput of thousands of frames per second without physics. Adding segmentation rendering introduced less than a 1% overhead.

### 4.4 Agreement with analytical solutions
Alloy was tested against 10 benchmarks with closed-form theoretical solutions, covering rigid friction, elastic rod bending, torsion, deflection, buckling, hydrostatic pressure, and soft-body stress. All measurements fell within pre-set tolerance bands, validating fundamental physical accuracy.

### 4.5 Reliability test across 1,024 worlds
Towers of 10 stacked 5 cm blocks were simulated for 5 seconds across 1,024 parallel worlds, with initial position offsets up to 0.5 mm. In this demanding test—where a block shifting over 1 cm or generating non-finite numbers is marked an error—the failure rate was 0 across two trials (0 errors out of 1,024 worlds) across precision, default, and fast settings.

sections.heading: Current development status and things to keep in mind
sections.summary: Alloy is currently in its early 0.x release stage, and interfaces may evolve. Unsupported features and known limitations are cataloged in public documentation.
sections.details:
Alloy is under active development in its early 0.x release cycle, and API specifications may change based on community feedback.

Features that are not yet supported and constraints to watch out for are openly listed in the official documentation (https://alloy.argonrobotics.ai/docs/keep-in-mind/). Each entry outlines its impact and practical workarounds, ensuring full transparency for users.

sections.heading: A simulator opening a new era of multi-material, AI-driven robotics
sections.summary: Alloy brings diverse real-world materials into a single scene, enabling stable, large-scale training through automatic coupling and health monitoring. It is open-sourced as a physics engine built for both human researchers and AI agents.
sections.details:
Alloy moves robot learning simulation forward from rigid-only worlds to environments that capture the material richness of the real world. Cloth, cables, water, sand, and soft bodies surrounding a robot can now be handled within one framework, automatically routed to the right solvers, and coupled with adaptive time steps.

Continuous health checks on parallel worlds offer peace of mind, preventing simulation breakdowns from derailment. With in-package documentation and MCP support, autonomous AI coding agents have proven they can interact with the engine to train policies successfully. Released as an open-source tool, Alloy provides a strong foundation to accelerate future robotics research.

takeaways: Rigid bodies, cloth, cables, fluids, and soft bodies simulate in a single scene without manual glue code, fully supporting existing MJCF robot assets.
Solver coupling is automated, dynamically calculating sub-step intervals based on contact stiffness and effective mass to drastically reduce parameter tuning.
Real-time health grading (OK, DEGRADED, INVALID) per world enables automatic rollbacks and freezes on physical breakdowns, preventing reinforcement learning reward hacking.
Engineered for coding agents (LLMs) with Model Context Protocol (MCP) support, JSON CLI tools, and error messages that suggest concrete fixes.
limitations: Alloy is in its early 0.x release stage, meaning interfaces and specifications may change in future updates.
Extremely large particle counts for fluids or granular materials and fine mesh resolutions may hit GPU memory and parallel scaling limits on a single card.
Certain edge cases and unsupported features remain, requiring users to consult the workarounds documented on the 'keep-in-mind' public page.
